note: strategic depth: auxiliary final-wall heads for long-horizon supervision, 1024-simulation policy targets via playout-cap randomization, and twice as many determinizations per refill
_note_why: run3, run4 and run5 all flattened out between +2250 and +2360, and Remi's verdict on run5 is specific and consistent across sessions: the TACTICS are good, the LONG-TERM PLAY is weak. Three things in the run5 stack point the same way, and run6 changes all three. (1) SUPERVISION IS SHORT-SIGHTED: the only labels are the outcome and the final margin, two numbers about the very end of the game, and nothing in the loss ever asks the net what SHAPE the game will end in. (2) THE HORIZON IS WASHED OUT BY CHANCE: every round boundary is a chance node re-sampled from only 4 determinizations, so a plan that pays off two rounds later is averaged over four guesses at each of two refills. (3) THE POLICY TARGET IS SHALLOW: 512 simulations resolve a tactical exchange but not a two-round plan, and the target is what the net imitates. Nothing here touches the net's capacity - run5 already showed capacity alone does not break the plateau.
_note_selfplay: Unchanged from run5: selfplay=batched runs `selfplay_games` games concurrently inside each of `workers` driver processes and puts every tree's next leaf into ONE forward pass on the GPU. 6 x 128 is run5's measured shape and run6 keeps it. Measured here, one driver, a full 128-game wave each, back to back on the same machine with run5 itself training throughout (so both rows carry the same competing load): run5's config 17.3 games/min/driver = 104 projected at 6 drivers, 4,046 positions/s, 257 evaluations/move; run6's config 13.4 games/min/driver = 80 projected, 3,085 positions/s, 254 evaluations/move. So run6 runs at 77% of run5's throughput - the cost is the 5.7% bigger net and the deeper trees, NOT more evaluations (254 against 257: playout-cap randomization plus tree reuse land almost exactly where run5's flat 512 did). 80 games/min still finishes 60k games comfortably. MPS driver allocation is 136.1 MB per driver either way. Each tree still searches strictly SEQUENTIALLY (search_batch=1); tests/test_selfplay_batched.py pins the equivalence, playout-cap randomization included - see that file for the honest boundary of the bit-identity claim.
_note_net: run5's architecture exactly - 7.04M parameters, 4 attention layers at width 256, 8 heads, 3x feed-forward, body 1536 - plus `aux_heads`. Keeping the shape identical is the point: run6 is a change of SUPERVISION, and an Elo difference is only attributable to it if the net is the same one. The pretraining warm start from run5's own buffer is also only as good as it is because the shapes match tensor for tensor.
_note_aux: THE MAIN CHANGE. 30 sigmoid outputs off the same body, predicting for BOTH players which wall rows (5), columns (5) and colours (5) their FINAL wall will hold - the game's whole end-of-game bonus structure, written out per set instead of summed. Targets come from the true final walls (AzulState.wall_summary) and are stored as 30 bits per position in the replay buffer, so the whole thing costs 4 bytes a position on disk and two Linears in the net. Why this and not more capacity or more simulations: whether row 3 ends up closed is decided FIVE ROUNDS after the position being labelled, so fitting it is impossible without carrying a plan, whereas the value head can be right about a position by reading the next exchange. It is the same argument AlphaGo made for its territory head and KataGo for ownership/score - auxiliary targets that share a trunk buy far more than their parameter count suggests, because they change what the trunk has to represent. aux_weight 0.1 is deliberately small: this is a REGULARISER on the trunk, not a second objective, and the policy/value losses must stay in charge (the aux BCE starts at ln 2 = 0.69, so the weighted term opens at ~0.07 against a total loss of a few units). Cost: 401k parameters (two Linears, 7.04M -> 7.44M, +5.7%), 4 bytes a position on disk, and nothing at all in the search - the head is never evaluated during a search, so visit counts and policy targets are bit-identical to what a head-free net would have produced.
_note_pcr: Playout-cap randomization, from KataGo. Each self-play MOVE independently draws a deep search (1024 simulations, root Dirichlet noise, visit distribution recorded as a policy target) with probability 0.25, and a cheap one (256 simulations, NO root noise) otherwise; a cheap move still enters the buffer with its value, margin and aux labels - those come from the end of the game, not from the search - but with NO policy target and a zeroed policy_mask, so it contributes no policy gradient at all. The arithmetic is the whole point: expected simulations per move is 0.25 x 1024 + 0.75 x 256 = 448, BELOW run5's flat 512, so the policy targets get twice run5's depth and the game volume is not paid for. Tree reuse makes it cheaper still - a cheap search that follows a full one inherits a root that is already past 256 visits and runs zero new simulations. Root noise only on full searches is KataGo's rule and matters here: noise exists to diversify the positions that become TARGETS, and a cheap move is not one.
_note_search: sims MUST equal pcr.full_sims (the trainer refuses otherwise): the full search IS the configured search, and everything that reads `sims` - the tree-reuse budget, the log line - has to agree with it. chance_children goes 4 -> 8, which is the second horizon change: a refill edge's Q is the visit-weighted mean over the determinizations sampled below it (chance_backup 'mean' - that is not a new rule, it is what the shared edge counters have always produced, and tests/test_train_mcts.py proves the identity numerically rather than asserting it in prose), so doubling the sample halves the variance of every cross-round comparison the search makes. Measured cost, isolating the search with a stub evaluator so the GPU and the machine's other load are out of the picture (12 near-round-end positions, 1024 simulations each, three repeats): 42.9 ms/search at 4 against 44.8 ms at 8, i.e. +4.4% of the Python descent, with non-overlapping spreads. Nodes per search are IDENTICAL (1025 either way) because the tree size is bounded by the simulation count, not by the width of the chance sample - so the memory cost is exactly zero, and MPS driver allocation is 136.1 MB at 128 concurrent games with either setting. The descent is about a third of a batched driver's wall clock, so end to end this is ~1.5%: the full-wave measurement could not distinguish it from noise. Everything else is run5's: c_puct, the noise, tree reuse, the temperature schedule.
_note_pretrain: run5's buffer: 500k positions played at 512 sims by a ~2290-Elo net of the SAME architecture, carrying native `margins` and `margin_mask` (value_score_weight was already 0 when it was written, so pretrain_unblend MUST stay 0 - running run4's 0.15 recovery on these values would fabricate margins from nothing). What it does NOT carry is aux targets, and that is handled rather than worked around: those positions load with a zero `aux_mask` and the aux loss skips them entirely, so three epochs fit the policy, value and margin heads to everything run5 knows while the strategic heads stay at their initialisation and start learning from run6's own first games. Same for `policy_mask`, which defaults to 1 for a file written before cheap searches existed - every run5 position has a real 512-sim target.
_note_loop: games_per_iter 768 = workers x selfplay_games, one full wave of concurrent games per iteration, exactly as run5. eval_every_games matches it so a checkpoint lands on an iteration boundary.
_note_lr: Unchanged from run5, and the arithmetic is unchanged with it: 60000 games x 52 positions x 1.5 replays / 256 per batch = ~18.3k self-play steps, so lr_total_steps=18500 lands the cosine on lr_min at the end of the game budget. Playout-cap randomization does not change positions per game - every move still produces a training position, only 25% of them carry a policy target - so the step budget is the same one. Peak 5e-4, lr_min 5e-5, as run5.
_note_anchors: run1 (+2014), run2 (+2020.3), run3 (+2254.7, re-rated) and run4 (+2360.6, re-rated) are pinned so run6's curve shares the scale every earlier run was measured on. ADD RUN5'S BEST HERE AT LAUNCH: append "mcts:runs/run5/checkpoints/ckpt-XXXXXX.pt?sims=100" to eval_anchors and the same string with its Elo to anchor_elos. Do NOT take that Elo from the best line of runs/run5/elo.jsonl - with dozens of evaluations at +/-25 Elo each, the maximum of the series is an order statistic and overstates the truth by roughly the noise. Re-rate it first against the anchors that are already on the scale and paste the fitted number: nice -n 19 uv run python -m ludometer.eval.gauntlet --games 40 --workers 8 --seed 6161 --json runs/run5/rerate.json --anchor run3=2254.7 --anchor run4=2360.6 run3=mcts:runs/run3/checkpoints/ckpt-020992.pt?sims=100 run4=mcts:runs/run4/checkpoints/ckpt-037888.pt?sims=100 run5a=mcts:runs/run5/checkpoints/ckpt-003072.pt?sims=100 run5b=mcts:runs/run5/checkpoints/ckpt-003840.pt?sims=100 -- 6 pairings x 40 = 240 games; swap run5a/run5b for whichever two checkpoints top runs/run5/elo.jsonl when run5 actually finishes, and anchor on the better of the two.
